patient.chief_complaint: Sudden-onset double vision when looking at distant objects, worsening over 3 weeks
patient.history_present_illness: A 29-year-old right-handed woman presents to the neurology inpatient service after referral from ophthalmology for evaluation of acute-onset horizontal diplopia. The patient reports that approximately 3 weeks ago, she began noticing double vision when looking at distant objects, particularly when watching television or looking across a room. The diplopia is described as horizontal, with images side by side, and resolves completely when she covers either eye. She notes the symptoms are intermittent and seem to worsen during periods of stress or fatigue, and she has noticed improvement on weekends when she is more relaxed. Near vision activities such as reading on her phone or computer do not provoke diplopia. She denies any associated headache, nausea, vomiting, or change in vision clarity. There is no history of recent head trauma, febrile illness, or new medications. She reports increased daily screen time over the past several months due to remote work, averaging 10 to 12 hours per day on digital devices. The patient was initially evaluated by ophthalmology, who documented intermittent comitant esotropia of 25 to 30 prism diopters at distance and variable measurements at near, with full ocular ductions and no nystagmus. The ophthalmologist noted that the esotropia was inconsistently present during different portions of the examination, with periods of normal alignment. Given her childhood history of strabismus surgery and the acute presentation, she was referred to neurology to exclude intracranial pathology. The patient reports significant psychosocial stress over the past year, including a difficult divorce, workplace instability, and estrangement from a family member. She endorses poor sleep quality with early morning awakenings and intermittent episodes of palpitations and chest tightness over the past several months. She has a maternal aunt diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, which has been causing her considerable anxiety about her own neurological health.

results.title: Convergence spasm: a functional or organic disorder?
results.summary: Convergence spasm (also termed spasm of the near reflex) is characterized by intermittent episodes of convergence, miosis, and accommodative spasm. While historically attributed to organic posterior fossa lesions, the majority of cases in modern series are functional in nature. Key distinguishing features include intermittency, variability during examination, and resolution with monocular viewing. The triad of convergence, miosis, and accommodative spasm during episodes is a characteristic clinical pattern.

results.title: Functional visual symptoms in neurology: a practical approach
results.summary: Functional visual symptoms including diplopia, visual field deficits, and convergence spasm are increasingly recognized as part of the FND spectrum. Diagnosis should be made on positive clinical signs (inconsistency, incongruity with anatomical patterns) rather than by exclusion. Convergence spasm producing intermittent esotropia can be identified by the accompanying miosis and accommodative effort, which distinguishes it from a true sixth nerve palsy.

results.title: Acute acquired comitant esotropia: differential diagnosis and management
results.summary: Acute acquired comitant esotropia (AACE) has multiple etiologies including digital device overuse, decompensated phoria, intracranial pathology, and functional causes. Convergence spasm should be considered when esotropia is intermittent, variable, and associated with miosis. MRI of the brain is recommended in all cases of AACE to exclude posterior fossa lesions, particularly in pediatric patients.

output.summary: Literature supports that convergence spasm presenting as intermittent comitant esotropia is most commonly functional in modern case series. Posterior fossa lesions are reported in a minority of cases and MRI is recommended in the evaluation of acute acquired comitant esotropia. The characteristic clinical pattern includes convergence, miosis, and accommodative spasm during episodes. Diagnosis relies on positive signs of inconsistency and incongruity.

differential.key_features: Sensorimotor symptoms in a young adult raise demyelinating disease; brain (and when indicated spine) MRI without T2/FLAIR lesions or enhancement argues against an active demyelinating process.
Sudden focal deficit raises stroke; non-anatomical weakness pattern with positive Hoover sign, normal MRI/DWI, and intact reflexes argue against vascular etiology.
Focal complaints warrant imaging; normal brain MRI without lesion, mass, or enhancement effectively excludes a structural cause for the presenting deficit.
Episodic neurological symptoms can occur in autoimmune encephalitis; normal MRI, normal EEG background, and (when obtained) negative antibody panel render this very unlikely.

useless_tools.rationale: Echocardiography has no role in FND; no structural cardiac question is raised by the presentation.
Cardiac rhythm monitoring is not indicated; the events are non-syncopal and the rule-in signs point to FND.
Non-contrast head CT adds no information beyond MRI for an FND workup and contributes diagnostic noise plus radiation exposure.
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in typical FND; invasive testing reinforces somatic illness model and adds iatrogenic risk without changing management.
Advanced PET imaging has no indication in FND; standard MRI is the appropriate structural workup.

Nerve conduction studies and EMG have no role once positive functional signs are documented: the deficit is not neuromuscular, the study is uncomfortable, and a normal result reinforces the patient's search for an organic cause — the principal iatrogenic harm in this condition
Somatosensory evoked potentials answer a question about a lesion in the somatosensory pathway; a midline-splitting, non-anatomical sensory deficit is not that question

critical_actions: Do NOT make the diagnosis by exclusion: document at least one positive rule-in sign, which is the act that establishes it
Communicate the diagnosis transparently using positive language and the rule-in signs as the basis
Refer for FND-informed physiotherapy and CBT / psychological therapy
Order a comprehensive neuropsychological battery to characterize comorbid depression, anxiety, somatization, and trauma exposure — informs treatment planning (criteria-pack 'recommended' tier)
contraindicated_actions: Do not pursue ever-expanding negative investigations — per Stone 2018, repeated negative workups reinforce illness conviction and worsen prognosis
Do not frame the diagnosis as 'all in your head', 'nothing wrong', or 'we couldn't find anything' — this damages the therapeutic alliance and is the most common avoidable harm in FND
Do not perform invasive testing (lumbar puncture, nerve biopsy, muscle biopsy, cerebral angiography) when positive rule-in signs are present and there is no clinical indication
Do not order EMG/NCS, muscle biopsy, or nerve biopsy as part of an FND workup — these invasive tests reinforce the somatic illness model per Stone 2018
Do not give gadolinium without a specific indication — contrast adds cost and risk and answers no question that positive functional signs have not already answered

Do not repeat the brain MRI, the laboratory panel or the lumbar puncture once a first normal study and positive rule-in signs are documented: each repetition strengthens the patient's belief that something organic has been missed
key_reasoning_points: FND is a positive diagnosis based on rule-in signs (Hoover, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline split) — not a diagnosis of exclusion (Espay 2018, Stone 2018).

Brain MRI and basic laboratory testing are OPTIONAL here, not due diligence: the diagnosis rests on the positive signs, and each additional negative study is a cost and an iatrogenic harm rather than a confirmation. Where imaging is recommended in this case it is for one specific alternative question, once.
Over-investigation is the principal iatrogenic harm in FND; every additional negative test reinforces the patient's illness conviction and worsens prognosis (Stone 2018).
Psychiatric comorbidity (anxiety, depression, trauma) is common and informs treatment planning but is NOT required for the diagnosis and does not 'explain' the symptoms in a reductive sense.
Diagnostic communication matters: using positive language anchored on the rule-in signs is associated with better engagement and outcomes (Stone 2018).
Evidence-based treatment is multidisciplinary — CBT for PNES and FND-informed physiotherapy for functional motor symptoms (Nielsen 2015).

red_herrings.data_point: Family history of multiple sclerosis in a relative
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on a demyelinating diagnosis (MS) and pursue extensive MS-specific workup before considering FND
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Non-first-degree family history of MS is a weak risk factor; the patient's symptoms must be evaluated on positive findings. Normal brain MRI without demyelinating lesions effectively addresses this concern.

red_herrings.data_point: Family history of epilepsy in a relative
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on an epileptic etiology and pursue prolonged AED trials before confirming PNES with video-EEG
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Family history of epilepsy does not establish the patient's events as epileptic. Video-EEG capturing the habitual event without ictal correlate is the gold standard.

red_herrings.data_point: Pre-existing psychiatric diagnosis (anxiety or depression) in the past medical history
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. Diagnosis requires positive rule-in signs on examination; psychiatric history is relevant for treatment planning, not for diagnosis.

red_herrings.data_point: Symptom onset coincident with a major psychosocial stressor
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude prematurely that stress 'caused' the symptoms and that the workup can be abbreviated
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions (MS, migraine, epilepsy) also flare with stress. Stress at onset is supportive context, not a diagnostic substitute for the positive rule-in signs.

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty due to multiple confounding factors: childhood strabismus history suggesting recurrence, high screen time suggesting digital device-related AACE, incidental white matter lesion raising MS concern, mildly elevated TSH as metabolic red herring, and family history of MS increasing patient and clinician anxiety. The convergence spasm pattern with miosis and midline vibratory splitting provide positive functional signs, but require careful neuro-ophthalmological reasoning to identify.
